title: Visualize insertion and selection sort
audience: Students with basic programming knowledge who are new to assembly
learningObjectives: Call and test a leaf renderer through an explicit register contract
Render offset-encoded signed bars with active-prefix bounds
Compare native instruction and branch counts with stated measurement scope

quiz.prompt: Is an array of zeroes a correct result for every input?

choices.text: No; it can lose the original values.
Yes, because all entries are equal.
Only if the frame is white.

hints.text: Check multiplicities as well as adjacent order.
The inactive suffix is outside the sorting domain and remains unchanged.

quiz.prompt: How tall is the bar for value zero?

choices.text: Zero cells.
Five cells.
Eight cells.

hints.text: Apply the encoding rather than interpreting height as signed magnitude.
Value −4 lights only row seven; value three lights all eight rows.

steps.title: Initialize inputs and publish the initial call

quiz.prompt: Why keep sorting state in saved registers across the call?

choices.text: The renderer contract preserves them while temporary registers are scratch.
All registers automatically restore after `jal`.
The simulator forbids temporary registers.

hints.text: A function call transfers control; its register effects come from a contract.
The renderer stub returns to main, but no correct image exists until its body is filled.

From the link address established by the caller.
From the last array value.

steps.title: Draw one column cell with a bounds check

quiz.prompt: Why test x<count before loading?

choices.text: To make every value positive.
To stop the whole program on column zero.
The inactive tail is not an input to this render call.

hints.text: A callable function may receive a shorter prefix or an offset pointer.

quiz.prompt: Why store black on every render?

choices.text: A bar may shrink or a column may become inactive.

hints.text: An old frame is persistent memory.

quiz.prompt: What would expose a hidden dependency on `s0` as the input pointer?

choices.text: Only testing the default main call.
Calling render directly with `a0` set and `s0` holding an unrelated value.
Changing a comment.

hints.text: A public argument should determine behavior without undocumented globals.
All saved registers and `sp` retain their caller values; only the frame changes.

quiz.prompt: Why use separate algorithms under one visualization contract?

choices.text: They must have equal instruction counts.
They require the same private registers.
Their observed states can be compared under the same frame and preservation rules.

hints.text: Keep the observable interface stable while changing the algorithm.
Each valid selector enters its own loop setup.

quiz.prompt: What is the sorted-prefix invariant before an insertion?

choices.text: The items before the new outer index are already ordered.
Every unvisited item is zero.
The whole array is always reversed.

hints.text: The outer loop adds one item to a known prefix.
Empty and singleton inputs exit without loading a pair.

quiz.prompt: Why is the comparison strict?

choices.text: Equal items must always exchange.
Equal keys need not cross each other in this insertion variant.
Strict comparison ignores negative values.

hints.text: Consider two equal keys carrying different identity tags.
For the default first pair, −2 is smaller than 2, so an exchange is required.

quiz.prompt: Why are both values loaded before either is overwritten?

choices.text: To preserve the frame base.
To avoid every branch.
The second old value would otherwise be lost.

hints.text: An exchange is a permutation, not two copies of one value.
The first snapshot after an exchange is [−2,2,3,−4,0,1,−3,−1], with `swap_count` one.

quiz.prompt: What guarantees progress after an insertion finishes?

choices.text: The outer index increases toward count.
The renderer increments every array value.
The algorithm selector changes.

hints.text: Separate the two loop variants.
Insertion sort now handles the active prefix completely.

quiz.prompt: How many adjacent exchanges does this insertion policy need on already sorted input?

choices.text: Twenty-eight.
Zero.
One for every equal pair.

hints.text: There is no inverted adjacent pair to exchange.
The default has seventeen inversions; eight distinct reversed values have twenty-eight.

quiz.prompt: Why can selection sort stop before scanning a final single item?

choices.text: It is always zero.
Its address is invalid.
Only one remaining item is already in its final suffix position.

hints.text: Use the established sorted prefix and remaining multiset.
For the default input, the initial candidate minimum is value two at index zero.

quiz.prompt: What happens when a later candidate equals the current minimum?

choices.text: Keep the earlier minimum index.
Choose the last equal candidate.
Exchange immediately during the scan.

hints.text: The published policy specifies the first minimum.
The first default scan chooses index three, containing −4.

quiz.prompt: Why not publish a self-exchange?

choices.text: It changes the multiset.

hints.text: A pass can establish progress without a data exchange.
The first selection exchange gives [−4,−2,3,2,0,1,−3,−1].

quiz.prompt: What describes the prefix after each selection pass?

choices.text: It contains the most recently visited values in arbitrary order.
It contains only zeroes.

hints.text: Separate finding a minimum from extending the fixed prefix.

quiz.prompt: Does phase two imply one more exchange?

choices.text: No; it reports completion of the current array.

steps.title: Verify order and multiplicities at every snapshot

quiz.prompt: Why check intermediate permutations?

choices.text: Every temporary register must equal the reference.
A half-exchange or lost value can precede an apparently sorted final result.
It makes signed comparison unnecessary.

hints.text: Correct status metadata alone does not prove the corresponding array state.
A sorted array with lost duplicates or an altered inactive word is rejected.

quiz.prompt: Do the current value-only checks prove stability of arbitrary record sorting?

choices.text: Yes, because the numbers are ordered.
Yes, because tags are irrelevant.
No; record identities need their own representation and checks.

hints.text: Equal numeric values can hide a changed relative identity order.
Selection can turn [2a,2b,1] into [1,2b,2a]. The value array still reads [1,2,2].

quiz.prompt: Is `sort_ready` an atomic hardware swap instruction?

choices.text: No; it is a logical observation boundary after several instructions.
Yes, it updates both words simultaneously.
It exists only as a source comment.

hints.text: The boundary names when state is coherent; it does not combine earlier writes.
The selected frame is stable while paused; a full-speed Run may repaint fewer intermediate states.

The caller's in-range `jal` and `nop`.

hints.text: Filtering is by executed instruction address, not by a guessed algorithm category.
A large whole-run difference can be dominated by how many frames were rendered.

steps.title: Read branch totals with their definition

quiz.prompt: What does a taken-branch count measure?

choices.text: Prediction misses on a physical processor.
Host-time stalls.
Executed core branch decisions whose outcome was taken.

hints.text: A simulator decision stream is not a branch-predictor model.
The reference selection range executes 115 branch decisions on each measured eight-item ordering, with different directions.

quiz.prompt: Why must a performance comparison name the input?

choices.text: The work performed depends on its ordering and duplicate structure.
The ISA changes between arrays.
The frame size is random.

hints.text: State algorithm, input, metric, and included work together.
On sorted input insertion has lower measured sorting work; on reversed input the visualizer pays for many more insertion frames.
